summary: Yolo County's most disorienting statistic is its median age of 32.3 — one of the lowest in California — which makes sense the moment you remember that UC Davis, one of the largest universities in the UC system, anchors the county's economy and identity so thoroughly that the city of Davis alone accounts for roughly a third of the population. That university presence ripples outward: 44% of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher, agriculture and higher education are the twin economic engines, and the county seat of Woodland adds a layer of government and ag-processing employment. The landscape is Sacramento Valley floor — dead flat, open-sky farm horizons stretching west toward the Coast Range, spectacular winter sunsets over rice fields and tomato acreage. At 221 people per square mile across over a thousand square miles, the density is strikingly thin outside the two main towns. A median home value of $593,800 against $88,818 in household income yields a price-to-income ratio near 6.7, which puts ownership out of comfortable reach at the median — yet median rent at $1,757 stays noticeably below Sacramento's. Summers are blazing, with average highs well into the 90s and nearly ten hours of daily sunshine year-round, while winter nights dip into the 30s with thick tule fog. Davis offers exceptional bike infrastructure and trail connectivity; Woodland feels more car-oriented and fragmented by highway corridors. The defining tension is a county that produces world-class research and some of California's most valuable crops yet still carries a 16.3% poverty rate — intellectual and agricultural wealth flowing through a place where the economic floor remains stubbornly low.
